title: Sizes and types of firms
overview: Theme 3 opens by asking why firms are the size they are and who they are run for. Most UK businesses are tiny, yet a handful of giants dominate output in many markets. This topic explains why some firms stay small while others grow, how the separation of ownership from control in large companies creates the principal-agent problem, and how public sector and not-for-profit organisations differ from private, profit-seeking firms. These ideas feed directly into business objectives (3.2.1), growth (3.1.2) and market structures (3.4), so they appear across Paper 1 and Paper 3.
objectives: Explain at least five reasons why some firms remain small and why others grow large
Distinguish between public and private sector organisations and between profit and not-for-profit organisations, with UK examples
Explain the divorce of ownership from control and analyse the principal-agent problem in public limited companies
Evaluate how far the principal-agent problem can be reduced by incentive schemes, corporate governance and the market for corporate control
Link firm size to economies of scale, market size and owner objectives in extended answers

sections.heading: How firm size is measured
sections.body:
There is no single measure of size. Economists and governments use several, and they can give different rankings:

- **Number of employees**: the usual official measure. In the UK a micro business has 0–9 employees, a small business 10–49, a medium business 50–249 and a large business 250 or more. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are those with fewer than 250 employees.
- **Turnover (sales revenue)**: useful for comparing firms in the same industry, but a supermarket has huge turnover on thin margins while a software firm may have small turnover and high profit.
- **Market share**: the firm's sales as a percentage of total market sales. This measures market power rather than absolute size; a small brewery may dominate a local market.
- **Market capitalisation**: share price multiplied by the number of shares, for public limited companies only. It reflects expected future profits rather than current scale.
- **Capital employed**: the value of assets used. Capital-intensive firms such as energy companies look large on this measure even with few workers.

The UK business population is dominated by small firms. Government estimates put the number of private sector businesses at around 5.5 million in 2024, of which over 99% were SMEs and the vast majority were micro businesses, many with no employees at all. SMEs account for roughly three-fifths of private sector employment and around half of private sector turnover. Yet in markets such as grocery retailing, banking, mobile telecoms and energy supply, a few large firms account for most sales. Good answers notice this paradox: small firms dominate by number, large firms dominate by output in many industries.

sections.heading: Why some firms remain small
sections.body:
Small firms survive alongside giants for both demand-side and supply-side reasons.

- **Small market size**: if the market is small, local or niche (a village hairdresser, a specialist bike-frame builder), there is simply not enough demand to support a large firm. Growth would mean producing output nobody wants.
- **Low minimum efficient scale (MES)**: in many service industries, economies of scale are exhausted at a low output. A plumber or a café reaches the lowest point of its long-run average cost curve with a few employees, so a large rival has no cost advantage.
- **Product differentiation and personal service**: customers may value bespoke products, flexibility and personal relationships that large bureaucratic firms find hard to offer.
- **Owner objectives**: many owners are satisficers who value independence, control and work-life balance more than maximum profit. They may deliberately avoid growth that would require outside shareholders or professional managers.
- **Lack of access to finance**: banks see small firms as risky because they have little collateral and short trading records, so loans are costly or unavailable. Small firms cannot issue shares on a stock exchange.
- **Government support and niche protection**: small firms benefit from schemes such as the VAT registration threshold (£90,000 of turnover from April 2024), Start Up Loans and business rates relief, which reduce their costs relative to larger rivals.
- **Flexibility**: small firms can adapt quickly to changes in tastes and avoid diseconomies of scale such as communication and coordination problems.

Some small firms are also new firms on their way to becoming large: today's start-up may be tomorrow's market leader, so the size distribution changes over time.

sections.heading: Why other firms grow large
sections.body:
Firms grow because growth usually raises profit, security or the rewards of the people running them.

- **Economies of scale**: as output rises, long-run average cost falls through technical, purchasing, managerial, financial, marketing and risk-bearing economies. Where MES is high, as in car production, steel, pharmaceuticals or mobile networks, only large firms can produce at competitive cost.
- **Market power**: a larger market share gives the firm more control over price, allowing it to raise price above marginal cost and earn supernormal profit. It also gives monopsony power over suppliers.
- **Survival and security**: large, diversified firms are less exposed to a downturn in any one market and are harder to take over.
- **Managerial objectives**: managers' salaries, status and power tend to rise with the size of the firm rather than with its profit, so managers may push for growth even if shareholders would prefer higher dividends (see the principal-agent problem below).
- **Network effects**: in digital platforms the product becomes more valuable as more people use it, so markets tend to tip towards one or two very large firms.
- **Access to global markets**: the internet and falling trade costs allow successful firms to sell across borders, multiplying the potential market.

The balance of these forces explains the size structure of an industry. Where MES is low relative to market demand, many small firms coexist. Where MES is high relative to demand, the industry tends towards oligopoly or even natural monopoly.

sections.heading: Public and private sector organisations
sections.body:
The **private sector** consists of organisations owned by private individuals or groups: sole traders, partnerships, private limited companies (Ltd) and public limited companies (plc), as well as private not-for-profit bodies such as charities. Private sector firms are usually financed by owners' capital, retained profit and borrowing.

The **public sector** consists of organisations owned or controlled by the state, at central or local level. Examples include government departments, the NHS, state schools, local councils and public corporations such as the BBC, Channel 4 and Network Rail. Public sector organisations are financed mainly by taxation, borrowing and, for public corporations, by charges and licence fees.

The key differences are:

- **Objectives**: private firms usually seek profit; public sector bodies pursue social objectives such as universal access, equity, or the provision of public and merit goods, often subject to a budget constraint.
- **Accountability**: private firms answer to shareholders; public bodies answer to ministers, Parliament and voters.
- **Discipline**: a loss-making private firm eventually exits the market; a public body may be bailed out, which can weaken the incentive to control costs (a source of X-inefficiency).

The boundary moves over time. Privatisation in the 1980s and 1990s transferred British Telecom, British Gas, the water companies and the railways to the private sector, and Royal Mail was privatised in 2013. More recently the direction has partly reversed: rail franchises have been taken back into public ownership as contracts expire, with the plan to bring passenger services together under Great British Railways, and the government took control of British Steel's Scunthorpe operations in 2025 under emergency legislation. These cases are useful evidence when evaluating state versus private ownership.

sections.heading: Profit and not-for-profit organisations
sections.body:
A **profit-making organisation** aims to generate a surplus of revenue over costs that is distributed to its owners (as dividends or drawings) or retained for growth.

A **not-for-profit organisation** may still earn a surplus, but the surplus is reinvested in the organisation's purpose rather than distributed to private owners. Examples include:

- **Charities** such as Oxfam, Cancer Research UK and the National Trust, which pursue social aims and are regulated by the Charity Commission.
- **Social enterprises** such as The Big Issue, which trade commercially but use their surplus for a social mission.
- **Mutuals and co-operatives** such as Nationwide Building Society and the Co-operative Group, owned by members rather than outside shareholders. Profits are returned to members through better rates, lower prices or dividends linked to use, rather than to investors.

Why does this distinction matter for economics? Because the theory of the firm in Theme 3 mostly assumes profit maximisation. A charity or mutual may instead aim to maximise output, quality or member welfare subject to breaking even, so it may produce more and charge less than a profit maximiser. Not-for-profit status can also build trust where consumers cannot easily judge quality (care homes, nurseries), since there is less incentive to cut corners for profit. On the other hand, the absence of shareholders seeking returns can weaken the pressure to minimise costs.

Note the difference between **ownership** and **objective**: an employee-owned firm such as the John Lewis Partnership is in the private sector and does aim to make profit, but distributes it to its employee-partners rather than outside shareholders. Not-for-profit does not mean public sector, and public sector does not always mean not-for-profit.

sections.heading: The divorce of ownership from control and the principal-agent problem
sections.body:
In a sole trader business the owner also runs the firm. As firms grow and become public limited companies, ownership is spread across thousands of shareholders (often pension funds and other institutions), while day-to-day control passes to professional directors and managers. This is the **divorce (or separation) of ownership from control**.

The **principal-agent problem** arises when one party (the agent) acts on behalf of another (the principal) but has different objectives and better information. Here the shareholders are the principals and the managers are the agents. Shareholders generally want profit maximisation, because that maximises dividends and share value. Managers may prefer:

- **Revenue or sales growth**, because pay, status and power rise with the size of the firm.
- **Perks and a quiet life**, accepting higher costs than necessary (X-inefficiency).
- **Short-term results** that trigger bonuses, rather than long-term investment.

The problem persists because of **asymmetric information** (managers know far more about the firm than dispersed shareholders) and the **free-rider problem** among shareholders (each small shareholder gains little from spending time monitoring managers, so few do).

Solutions include: aligning incentives through share options and performance-related pay; non-executive directors and the UK Corporate Governance Code; binding shareholder votes on directors' pay policy; active institutional investors; and the threat of takeover, since an underperforming firm has a low share price and becomes a target. Each has limits. Share options can encourage short-termism or risky behaviour to lift the share price before options vest; non-executives may be friends of the chief executive; and takeovers are themselves often driven by managers' empire-building. The principal-agent problem is therefore a key reason why the assumption of profit maximisation may not hold for large firms.

key_terms.definition: A business with fewer than 250 employees; micro businesses have fewer than 10, small fewer than 50 and medium fewer than 250.
A firm's sales as a percentage of the total sales in the market, measured by value or volume.
The lowest level of output at which long-run average cost is minimised.
The part of the economy owned and controlled by private individuals and organisations rather than the state.
Organisations owned or controlled by central or local government, financed mainly through taxation and government borrowing.
A state-owned trading organisation, such as the BBC or Network Rail, that provides goods or services and is run at arm's length from government.
An organisation that reinvests any surplus in its purpose rather than distributing it to private owners, for example a charity, social enterprise or mutual.
An organisation owned by its members (customers or employees) rather than external shareholders, for example a building society.
The separation, typical of public limited companies, between the shareholders who own a firm and the directors and managers who run it.

A situation in which an agent acting on behalf of a principal pursues their own objectives because their interests differ and the principal cannot fully monitor the agent due to asymmetric information.
Aiming for a satisfactory level of performance, such as a minimum acceptable profit, rather than the maximum, to balance the interests of different stakeholders.

diagrams.title: Why small firms can survive: low MES
diagrams.caption: Where economies of scale run out at a low output (Q1), as in hairdressing or cafés, small firms are as efficient as large ones and can coexist. Where MES is high (Q2), as in car making, small firms face much higher average costs and the industry tends to be dominated by large firms.

applications: UK business population: government estimates for 2024 put the number of private sector businesses at around 5.5 million, over 99% of them SMEs. Small firms are concentrated in construction, professional services and retail of personal services, where minimum efficient scale is low and local knowledge matters; large firms dominate capital-intensive or network industries such as energy, telecoms, banking and supermarkets.

Public versus private: the return of rail passenger services to public ownership as franchises expire, the planned creation of Great British Railways and the government taking control of British Steel's Scunthorpe works in 2025 show that the public-private boundary is a live policy choice. Supporters argue public ownership allows social objectives such as service levels and jobs; critics point to weaker cost discipline and the burden on public finances.

Mutuals and not-for-profits: Nationwide, the largest UK building society, is owned by its members rather than shareholders and in 2024 acquired Virgin Money, a profit-seeking bank, showing that mutuals can grow by acquisition too. Charities such as the National Trust run large commercial operations (cafés, shops, membership) but reinvest the surplus in their conservation purpose.

Principal-agent problem in UK plcs: shareholder votes against executive pay packages at FTSE 100 annual general meetings are a recurring story, and the UK Corporate Governance Code requires boards to include independent non-executive directors and remuneration committees. The debate over large pay awards at some water companies while they missed environmental targets illustrates how managers' rewards can diverge from the interests of owners and customers.

Global: Alphabet (Google), Meta and Amazon grew to enormous size because digital markets combine very high fixed costs with near-zero marginal costs and strong network effects, so MES is enormous relative to any single national market. Some of these firms also use dual-class share structures that keep founders in control, an alternative answer to the divorce of ownership from control.
evaluation: Size depends on the measure used: a firm can be small by employment but large by market share in a niche, so conclusions about market power should use market share in the relevant (possibly local) market, not employee numbers.

The significance of the principal-agent problem depends on how concentrated ownership is. Where a founder or a few institutions hold large stakes, monitoring is easier and managers have less freedom than where shares are widely dispersed.

Incentive schemes can reduce the principal-agent problem but create new ones: share options may encourage short-termism, buybacks to lift the share price or excessive risk-taking, as seen in the banking sector before 2008.

Small firms are not necessarily less efficient. If MES is low, they produce at minimum average cost and are often more dynamically efficient and innovative in niches; but in high-MES industries they face a structural cost disadvantage that no amount of effort can overcome.

Public ownership is not automatically less efficient than private ownership; the outcome depends on regulation, the degree of competition and management incentives. A private monopoly with weak regulation may perform worse than a well-run public body.

Over time, the size distribution of firms is changing: digital technology lowers costs for small firms (online marketplaces, cloud software), yet also creates platform giants with network effects, so the net effect differs by industry.
misconceptions: Thinking not-for-profit organisations never make a surplus. They often do; the difference is that the surplus is reinvested in their purpose rather than distributed to private owners.
Confusing a public limited company (plc) with the public sector. A plc is a privately owned company whose shares can be sold to the public; it is in the private sector.
Assuming large firms always have lower costs. Beyond MES, diseconomies of scale can raise average costs, and in low-MES industries large size brings no cost advantage at all.

Describing the principal-agent problem simply as 'managers are lazy'. The precise analysis is that objectives differ and information is asymmetric, so principals cannot fully monitor or enforce their objectives.
exam_tips: Section A short questions often ask you to explain one reason why firms remain small or define the principal-agent problem. Always give a precise definition, then apply it to the firm or industry in the question for the application mark.
When explaining why a firm stays small, link to a cost curve where possible: a low MES relative to market size is the most analytical reason and can be shown on an LRAC diagram.

In 25-mark essays on business objectives or mergers, use the principal-agent problem as a chain of analysis: separation of ownership and control, different objectives, asymmetric information, managers pursue growth or revenue, outcome for shareholders and consumers.
For evaluation, consider who owns the firm (dispersed or concentrated shareholdings), the effectiveness of governance mechanisms, and the type of industry (high or low MES).
Use precise UK categories: sole trader, partnership, Ltd, plc, public corporation, charity, mutual. Mixing them up loses knowledge marks.

model_answer.question: Evaluate the view that the principal-agent problem means large public limited companies are unlikely to maximise profits. (15 marks)
model_answer.answer:
A public limited company is owned by shareholders but run by directors and managers. This divorce of ownership from control creates a principal-agent problem: the shareholders (principals) want profit maximisation, where marginal cost equals marginal revenue, because this maximises dividends and the value of their shares, but the managers (agents) may have different objectives and know far more about the business than the owners do.

Managers' pay, status and power are often linked to the size of the firm rather than to its profit. They therefore have an incentive to pursue revenue maximisation (where MR = 0) or sales maximisation (where AR = AC), both of which involve producing more and charging less than at the profit-maximising output. For example, a chief executive may push for an acquisition that increases turnover even if the price paid destroys shareholder value. Managers may also tolerate higher costs than necessary, such as generous perks or overstaffing, so that the firm operates above its lowest possible average cost curve. This X-inefficiency reduces profit at every output. Because ownership of a large plc is dispersed among thousands of shareholders and institutions, no single shareholder gains enough from monitoring managers to make it worthwhile: a free-rider problem. Asymmetric information makes monitoring harder still, since shareholders see only published accounts. Together these factors suggest profits will be lower than the maximum.

However, there are strong forces pushing managers back towards profit. First, pay structures increasingly link bonuses and share options to earnings per share and total shareholder return, aligning managers' interests with owners'. Second, the UK Corporate Governance Code requires independent non-executive directors and remuneration committees, and shareholders now have binding votes on pay policy. Third, and most importantly, there is a market for corporate control: if managers neglect profit, the share price falls below the value the firm could achieve, making it an attractive takeover target, after which the managers are likely to lose their jobs. Finally, in competitive markets a firm that does not minimise costs and earn at least normal profit will lose market share and may not survive, so the scope for managers to depart from profit maximisation is limited.

The extent of the problem therefore depends on several factors. It is greatest where shareholdings are widely dispersed, the firm has significant market power (so it can earn enough supernormal profit to absorb inefficiency) and takeover is unlikely because of the firm's sheer size. It is smaller where a few institutional investors hold large stakes, or where a founder retains control. Incentive schemes are also double-edged: share options linked to short-term share prices may encourage buybacks and cost-cutting at the expense of investment, so managers may maximise short-run rather than long-run profit, which is still a departure from shareholders' true interest.

Overall, the view is only partly correct. The principal-agent problem means large plcs are unlikely to maximise profit precisely, because managers have both the motive and the information advantage to pursue other goals. But governance and market pressures mean most plcs are likely to satisfice at a level of profit close enough to the maximum to keep shareholders content and avoid takeover. The problem is most serious for very large firms with market power in uncompetitive markets, which is exactly where the consumer is also most at risk.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: precise definitions of the divorce of ownership from control, principal-agent problem, profit, revenue and sales maximisation. Application: refers to plcs, UK governance code, takeovers and share options rather than generic firms. Analysis: developed chains linking asymmetric information and free-riding to managerial objectives, output and profit, including X-inefficiency. Evaluation: several counter-arguments (incentive alignment, governance, market for corporate control, competition) weighed, followed by 'it depends on' factors (ownership concentration, market power) and a supported final judgement. This meets Level 4 KAA and Level 3 evaluation.

check.q: Which of the following is a reason why a firm may remain small?
options: Its industry has a high minimum efficient scale
Its market is a small local niche
It has easy access to stock market finance
It benefits from large purchasing economies of scale
check.explanation: A small or niche market cannot support a large firm. A high MES, stock market access and purchasing economies all favour large firms.

check.q: In a public limited company, who are the principals in the principal-agent relationship between owners and managers?
check.explanation: Shareholders own the company and appoint managers (agents) to run it on their behalf.

check.q: Which organisation is in the public sector?
options: Public limited company listed on the London Stock Exchange
Building society owned by its members
Public corporation such as Network Rail
check.explanation: Public corporations are state-owned. A plc, a mutual and a charity are all in the private sector, even though the last two are not-for-profit.

check.q: Why does the principal-agent problem persist in firms with widely dispersed shareholdings?
options: Managers are legally required to maximise revenue
Each shareholder gains little from monitoring managers, and managers have better information
Shareholders prefer managers to pursue growth over profit
check.explanation: Free-riding among small shareholders and asymmetric information mean managers are weakly monitored, so they can pursue their own objectives.

check.q: A not-for-profit organisation differs from a profit-making firm mainly because it
options: never earns more revenue than its costs
is always owned by the government
reinvests any surplus in its purpose rather than distributing it to private owners
check.explanation: Not-for-profits can make a surplus and can trade, and most are in the private sector; the key feature is that surpluses are not distributed to private owners.

title: Business growth
overview: Firms can grow internally, by selling more of what they already make, or externally, by merging with or taking over other firms. This topic covers organic growth, the three forms of integration (horizontal, vertical and conglomerate), the reasons for each and their costs and benefits, and the constraints that stop firms growing. It is one of the most heavily examined areas of Theme 3: data-response questions on a proposed merger and 25-mark essays on whether a takeover should be allowed come up regularly, and they reward analysis linked to economies of scale, market power and the interests of consumers, workers and suppliers.
objectives: Define organic growth and explain its advantages and disadvantages compared with external growth
Distinguish between horizontal, forward vertical, backward vertical and conglomerate integration using UK examples
Analyse the reasons for each type of integration, linking to economies of scale, market power, security of supply and risk
Evaluate the costs and benefits of integration for firms, consumers, workers and suppliers, including the trade-off between cost savings and market power
Explain the constraints on growth: size of market, access to finance, owner objectives and regulation

sections.heading: Why firms want to grow
sections.body:
Before examining how firms grow, be clear about why. The main motives are:

- **Economies of scale**: a larger scale of production lowers long-run average cost, raising profit margins or allowing lower prices.
- **Market power**: a larger market share allows the firm to influence price, earn supernormal profit and reduce the threat from rivals. It may also give buying (monopsony) power over suppliers.
- **Diversification and risk reduction**: selling in more markets or more products reduces exposure to a downturn in one of them.
- **Survival**: larger firms are harder to take over and better able to withstand shocks.
- **Managerial motives**: managers' pay and status often rise with firm size, so growth may be pursued for its own sake (the principal-agent problem).

Growth can be **organic (internal)** or **external (inorganic)**, through **mergers** (two firms agree to combine into one) or **takeovers / acquisitions** (one firm buys a controlling stake in another, sometimes against the wishes of the target's managers). Exam answers should make clear which route is being discussed, because the costs, risks and speed differ greatly.

sections.heading: Organic growth
sections.body:
**Organic growth** occurs when a firm expands using its own resources: increasing output, opening new outlets, developing new products, entering new markets or investing in new capacity. It is usually financed by retained profit or borrowing.

Greggs is a clear UK example: it has grown mainly by opening new shops, adding evening trading, delivery and drive-through sites, and now has more than 2,500 outlets. Many technology firms also grow organically by developing new features and attracting more users.

**Advantages**

- **Lower risk**: growth is gradual and builds on what the firm already does well, so managers understand the business.
- **No integration problems**: there is no clash of corporate cultures, IT systems or management structures.
- **Control is retained**: no need to issue large amounts of new shares or pay a takeover premium.
- **Less scrutiny from competition authorities**, because market share rises only by winning customers.

**Disadvantages**

- **Slow**: the firm may miss opportunities or be overtaken by rivals that grow by acquisition.
- **Limited by market growth**: in a mature, slow-growing market a firm can only grow organically by taking customers from rivals, which may trigger a price war.
- **Finance constraint**: relying on retained profit limits the pace of expansion, especially for small firms.
- **Lacks new capabilities**: buying another firm gives instant access to its technology, brands, staff and distribution, which organic growth may take years to build.

Organic growth also has a wider benefit: because new capacity is created, it tends to add to the economy's productive potential and competition, whereas a merger may simply combine existing capacity under one owner.

sections.heading: Horizontal integration
sections.body:
**Horizontal integration** is the combination of two firms in the same industry at the same stage of production, for example two mobile network operators or two supermarkets. Vodafone and Three merged their UK businesses in 2025 after the CMA approved the deal subject to commitments on network investment and prices; Nationwide's 2024 acquisition of Virgin Money combined two retail banks.

**Reasons and benefits**

- **Economies of scale**: the combined firm can rationalise production, close duplicate head offices and stores, buy in bulk and spread fixed costs such as IT and marketing over larger output. This shifts the firm down its LRAC curve.
- **Increased market share and market power**: fewer competitors means more control over price and potentially higher profits.
- **Eliminating a competitor** reduces rivalry and uncertainty.
- **Access to complementary assets**: customer bases, brands, spectrum or locations that are hard to build organically.

**Costs**

- **Higher prices and less choice for consumers** if market power is used rather than passed on as cost savings: allocative inefficiency and loss of consumer surplus.
- **Job losses** as duplicated roles and outlets are cut.
- **Monopsony power** over suppliers, who may receive lower prices.
- **Diseconomies of scale and integration problems**: culture clashes, incompatible systems and communication problems can mean promised cost savings never appear.
- **Reduced competitive pressure** can lead to X-inefficiency and less innovation over time.

Because horizontal mergers directly increase concentration, they receive the closest scrutiny from the Competition and Markets Authority. The CMA blocked the proposed Sainsbury's–Asda merger in 2019, concluding that it would lead to higher prices and lower quality for shoppers.

sections.heading: Vertical integration
sections.body:
**Vertical integration** is the combination of firms at different stages of the same production process (supply chain).

- **Backward vertical integration**: a firm merges with or acquires a supplier, moving towards raw materials. Examples: a streaming service producing its own films and series rather than licensing them; a car maker taking over a battery manufacturer.
- **Forward vertical integration**: a firm merges with or acquires a business closer to the final consumer, such as a manufacturer buying a retailer or a brewer owning pubs. Tesco's 2018 takeover of the wholesaler Booker is often analysed as an extension of the supply chain into wholesaling to independent shops and caterers.

**Reasons and benefits**

- **Security of supply** (backward) or **guaranteed outlets** (forward): reducing the risk that a supplier raises prices, cuts supply or favours a rival.
- **Cost savings**: removing the profit margin of the intermediate firm, lower transaction costs and better coordination of production and logistics.
- **Quality control** over inputs or over how the product is sold.
- **Capturing the profit** earned at other stages of the supply chain.
- **Barriers to entry**: controlling a key input or distribution channel can make it harder for rivals to compete.

**Costs**

- **Foreclosure**: the integrated firm may refuse to supply rivals or charge them more, reducing competition downstream or upstream. This was a key concern in the CMA's review of Microsoft's acquisition of Activision Blizzard, which it initially blocked in 2023 over cloud gaming before clearing a restructured deal.
- **Lack of expertise**: running a different stage of production requires different skills.
- **Reduced flexibility**: the firm is tied to its own supplier even if a cheaper or better outside supplier appears; internal suppliers lack competitive pressure (X-inefficiency).

sections.heading: Conglomerate integration
sections.body:
**Conglomerate integration** is the combination of firms producing unrelated products in different markets. Classic examples are Berkshire Hathaway (insurance, railways, energy, confectionery), the Tata Group (whose businesses include Jaguar Land Rover and Tata Steel) and the Virgin Group.

**Reasons and benefits**

- **Diversification of risk**: if demand falls in one market, profits from another can cushion the firm. Products with different cyclical patterns spread risk most effectively.
- **Growth when the core market is saturated** or where further horizontal growth would be blocked by competition authorities.
- **Financial and managerial economies of scale**: a large conglomerate can borrow more cheaply and spread head-office functions across divisions.
- **Using spare cash** from a mature, profitable business to invest in growing markets.

**Costs**

- **Lack of expertise and focus**: managers may not understand the new markets, leading to poor decisions.
- **Diseconomies of scale**: a sprawling group is harder to coordinate and control.
- **Few synergies**: there are rarely technical or purchasing economies between unrelated products, so cost savings are limited.
- **Shareholders can diversify themselves** more cheaply by holding a range of shares, so diversification within the firm may benefit managers (job security) more than owners. Stock markets often value conglomerates at less than the sum of their parts, the 'conglomerate discount', which is a major reason for demergers (3.1.3).

Conglomerate mergers rarely raise competition concerns because they do not increase market share in any single market, though very large conglomerates may use cross-subsidisation to undercut specialised rivals.

sections.heading: The trade-off for society: cost savings versus market power
sections.body:
The central economic question about a merger is whether the gains from lower costs outweigh the losses from greater market power. This is known as the **Williamson trade-off**.

Suppose, before the merger, an industry is competitive so price equals average and marginal cost at AC1. After the merger the combined firm achieves economies of scale, so costs fall to AC2, but it now has market power and sets output where MC = MR, raising price to P2. Two effects follow (see the diagram):

- **A gain**: the rectangle between AC1 and AC2 up to the new output is a saving in real resources. Society produces Q2 using fewer inputs.
- **A loss**: the triangle between the demand curve and AC1 from Q2 to Q1 is a deadweight welfare loss, because output has been restricted below the level at which price equals the original cost of production.

If the cost-saving rectangle is larger than the deadweight loss triangle, the merger raises total welfare even though consumers pay more. However, consumers lose surplus in both cases, so a merger can raise total welfare while harming consumers: the distributional effect matters. Competition authorities such as the CMA focus on consumer welfare and will usually block a merger, or require remedies such as selling stores, unless the efficiencies are large, verifiable and likely to be passed on in lower prices.

This framework gives you a structured Level 4 evaluation: the outcome **depends on** the size of the economies of scale, the price elasticity of demand (which determines the size of the deadweight loss), whether rivals or new entrants constrain price (contestability), and whether the promised savings actually materialise.

sections.heading: Constraints on business growth
sections.body:
Even firms that want to grow may be unable to. The specification lists four constraints:

- **Size of the market**: a firm cannot grow beyond what the market can absorb. Niche, local or declining markets (printed newspapers, letters) limit growth; global and growing markets allow it. Small market size relative to MES is why some industries can support only one or two firms.
- **Access to finance**: growth requires investment, financed by retained profit, borrowing or new shares. Small firms struggle to borrow because they lack collateral and track records, and cannot issue shares publicly. The rise in Bank Rate from 0.1% in late 2021 to 5.25% in 2023 raised borrowing costs for all firms and delayed many expansion plans; since cuts began in 2024 the constraint has eased somewhat.
- **Owner objectives**: owners may not want to grow. A family business may prefer control and a manageable workload; growth via issuing shares means sharing ownership and possibly losing control.
- **Regulation**: competition law limits growth through mergers. The CMA can investigate mergers that may substantially lessen competition and can block them or impose remedies, as with Sainsbury's–Asda (blocked in 2019) and Vodafone–Three (cleared with commitments). The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 gives the CMA extra powers over firms with strategic market status in digital markets. Other regulations, such as planning rules or sector licences, also constrain growth.

In addition, **diseconomies of scale** act as an internal constraint: beyond a point, coordination and motivation problems push up average costs and make further growth unprofitable. A good answer judges which constraint is most binding for the specific firm in the question.

key_terms.definition: Growth achieved by a firm expanding its own operations, such as increasing output, opening new outlets or developing new products, financed internally or by borrowing.
The agreed combination of two or more firms into a single business under common ownership.
The purchase of a controlling interest in one firm by another, which may be hostile or agreed.
The combination of firms in the same industry and at the same stage of production.
The combination of a firm with a business at an earlier stage of its supply chain, such as a supplier of raw materials or components.
The combination of a firm with a business at a later stage of its supply chain, closer to the final consumer, such as a manufacturer acquiring a retailer.
The combination of firms producing unrelated goods or services in different markets.
The extra value created when two firms combine, so that the merged firm is worth more than the two firms separately, usually through cost savings or revenue gains.
When a vertically integrated firm restricts rivals' access to an input or distribution channel it controls, reducing competition.
The comparison between the welfare gain from lower costs after a merger and the deadweight welfare loss from the higher price caused by greater market power.
The UK body that investigates mergers and markets and can block or impose conditions on mergers that would substantially lessen competition.

diagrams.title: Horizontal merger: moving down the LRAC
diagrams.caption: Two similar firms each producing Q1 merge and rationalise production, so the combined firm produces Q2 at a lower average cost AC2 by exploiting economies of scale. If the merged firm grew beyond the minimum point of the LRAC, diseconomies of scale would raise costs again.

diagrams.title: Williamson trade-off: cost savings vs market power
diagrams.caption: Before the merger, competition drives price down to cost at P1 and output Q1. The merged firm's costs fall to AC2, but it sets MC = MR, raising price to P2 and cutting output to Q2. The merger raises total welfare only if the cost-saving rectangle exceeds the deadweight loss triangle; consumers lose surplus either way.

formulae.name: Market share
formulae.example: A firm sells £120m in a £600m market: market share = 120 ÷ 600 × 100 = 20%.

formulae.name: n-firm concentration ratio
formulae.formula: Sum of the market shares of the n largest firms
formulae.example: Shares of 26%, 18%, 15% and 12% give a 4-firm ratio of 71%. If the second and fourth firms merge (30%), the next largest firm (10%) enters the top four: 30 + 26 + 15 + 10 = 81%.

applications: Horizontal: the CMA blocked the Sainsbury's–Asda merger in 2019 because it expected higher prices, reduced quality and less choice in many local areas and in fuel retailing. In contrast, it approved the Vodafone–Three merger in 2024 (completed in 2025) after the firms committed to a multi-billion-pound joint network investment plan and to caps on some tariffs for a period, judging that the investment benefits could outweigh the loss of a fourth competitor if the commitments were enforced.

Vertical: Microsoft's acquisition of the games publisher Activision Blizzard was initially blocked by the CMA in 2023 because of concerns that Microsoft could withhold games from rival cloud gaming services (foreclosure). The deal was cleared later in 2023 after it was restructured so that cloud streaming rights outside Europe were sold to Ubisoft, showing how remedies can address vertical concerns.

Organic: Greggs has grown mainly through opening new shops and extending trading hours and channels, reaching more than 2,500 outlets. Its growth shows the low-risk, gradual nature of organic growth, but also its limits: growth depends on finding good sites and on overall demand for food-to-go.

Conglomerate: the Tata Group is a highly diversified Indian conglomerate whose UK businesses include Jaguar Land Rover and Tata Steel. Diversification has allowed losses in one division to be absorbed by profits in another, while the conversion of Port Talbot's steelmaking to an electric arc furnace, with substantial UK government support, illustrates how conglomerates reallocate capital between businesses.

Global: the wave of consolidation in global brewing (AB InBev's acquisition of SABMiller in 2016) combined horizontal integration with forward integration into distribution. Competition authorities in several countries required disposals of brands before approval, showing that large horizontal mergers are increasingly cleared only with remedies.
evaluation: Size of the efficiency gains: merging firms often claim large synergies, but evidence suggests many mergers fail to deliver promised cost savings because of integration costs and diseconomies of scale. Claimed savings should be treated with caution unless they are specific and verifiable.

Whether savings are passed on to consumers depends on the remaining degree of competition and contestability. With strong rivals or low barriers to entry, the merged firm must pass on savings; with high market share and barriers, it is more likely to raise prices.

Time period: in the short run integration costs and redundancies may dominate; in the long run economies of scale and greater investment capacity (dynamic efficiency) may produce larger benefits, or reduced competition may lead to X-inefficiency.

Stakeholders: shareholders of the target usually gain (they receive a takeover premium) while shareholders of the acquirer often lose; workers may lose jobs through rationalisation; suppliers may face monopsony power; consumers may gain or lose depending on prices and quality.

Type of integration matters: horizontal mergers raise the greatest competition concerns; vertical mergers can reduce costs (eliminating double margins) but risk foreclosure; conglomerate mergers rarely harm competition but often destroy shareholder value because of lack of expertise.

Market definition: a merger that creates a high national market share may matter little if the market is global (e.g. car manufacturing), but local market concentration (towns with only two supermarkets) can matter more than national figures.
misconceptions: Confusing forward and backward vertical integration. Backward means moving towards raw materials (acquiring a supplier); forward means moving towards the final consumer (acquiring a distributor or retailer).

Assuming every merger leads to economies of scale. If the merged firm is already beyond minimum efficient scale, or the firms cannot integrate their operations, costs may rise through diseconomies of scale.
Writing that mergers always raise prices. If cost savings are large and competition remains, prices may fall; the outcome depends on the balance in the Williamson trade-off.

Thinking conglomerate integration produces technical economies of scale. Because the products are unrelated, the main economies are financial, managerial and risk-bearing, not technical or purchasing.
exam_tips: In data-response questions, identify the type of integration precisely and quote evidence from the extract (market shares, claimed savings, job cuts) to gain application marks.
Draw an LRAC diagram to show economies of scale from a merger, or the Williamson trade-off diagram for a higher-level analysis of welfare effects. Label AC1, AC2, P1, P2 and shade both areas.
Structure merger evaluation by stakeholder: shareholders, consumers, workers, suppliers and competitors. Then make a judgement about which effect is likely to dominate in this specific case.
Use the constraints on growth explicitly (size of market, access to finance, owner objectives, regulation) when asked why a firm might not grow, and judge which is the most significant for that firm.
Synoptic links score well: link mergers to concentration ratios (3.4.4), monopoly (3.4.5), contestability (3.4.7) and competition policy (3.6.1).

model_answer.question: A large UK supermarket chain plans to take over a national convenience-store chain. Evaluate the likely effects of this horizontal integration on consumers and on the firms involved. (25 marks)
model_answer.answer:
Horizontal integration is the combination of two firms at the same stage of production in the same industry. A supermarket taking over a convenience chain is horizontal because both are grocery retailers, though they serve partly different shopping missions: the large weekly shop versus top-up shopping.

For the firms, the main benefit is economies of scale. The combined firm can buy in larger volumes, so purchasing economies lower the cost of each item: a supermarket buying for thousands of extra stores can negotiate bigger discounts from food manufacturers. It can also spread fixed costs such as IT systems, distribution centres, marketing and head-office functions across a larger output, and close duplicate warehouses. This moves the firm down its long-run average cost curve from a point such as AC1 to a lower AC2, as in an LRAC diagram. With grocery profit margins typically thin, even small percentage cost savings can significantly raise profits. Second, the acquirer gains market share and access to a growing segment, as convenience shopping has expanded relative to large out-of-town stores. Buying an established chain is much faster than opening hundreds of new sites organically and gives immediate access to prime locations that rivals cannot replicate.

For consumers, the outcome depends on whether these cost savings are passed on. If the convenience chain's stores start selling the supermarket's own-label range at supermarket prices, shoppers could see lower prices and a wider range, raising consumer surplus. However, the merged firm also gains market power. In local markets, such as a small town where the two firms own the only large store and the only convenience shop, the merged firm faces less competition and can raise prices or reduce quality, service and opening hours without losing many customers because demand becomes more price-inelastic. This is shown by the Williamson trade-off: costs fall from AC1 to AC2, but if the firm sets MC = MR, price rises from P1 to P2 and output falls, creating a deadweight welfare loss. Consumers lose surplus even if total welfare rises because of the cost savings. Suppliers, such as farmers and small food producers, may also be squeezed by the merged firm's monopsony power, which could reduce their investment and in the long run the range of products available.

The overall effect depends on several factors. First, the degree of remaining competition: the UK grocery market includes several large chains and fast-growing discounters such as Aldi and Lidl, so nationally the merged firm's power to raise prices may be limited. But national figures can hide local monopolies, which is why the CMA examines overlap area by area and may require the sale of stores, as it found in the Sainsbury's–Asda case, which it blocked. Second, whether the economies of scale are real: many mergers fail to deliver promised savings because of integration costs, culture clashes and diseconomies of scale such as coordination problems in a much larger organisation. Third, the time period: in the short run consumers may benefit from price cuts as the firm seeks to win customers; in the long run, reduced competitive pressure may lead to X-inefficiency and less innovation. Fourth, for the acquiring firm itself, there is the risk of overpaying: the takeover premium paid to the target's shareholders may exceed the value of the synergies, so the acquirer's shareholders lose, which is common in practice and may reflect managers' empire-building (principal-agent problem).

On balance, the takeover is likely to benefit the firms through purchasing and distribution economies and access to the convenience segment, but the effect on consumers is ambiguous. Where there are many competitors locally and the discounters are a credible threat, cost savings are likely to be passed on and consumers may gain. Where the two chains overlap heavily in particular towns, consumers are likely to lose through higher prices and less choice. The most likely outcome is that the CMA would allow the deal only with remedies, such as selling stores in overlap areas, which would preserve most of the efficiency gains while limiting the abuse of market power. The key judgement therefore rests on local market concentration rather than the national picture.
model_answer.commentary: KAA Level 4: accurate definitions; application to grocery retail, convenience shopping, discounters and local overlap; developed chains on purchasing economies, fixed-cost spreading, market power, PED and monopsony; integrates the LRAC and Williamson trade-off diagrams. Evaluation Level 3: weighs cost savings against market power, considers whether savings are real, time period, stakeholders (consumers, suppliers, acquirer's shareholders) and regulation, and reaches a justified, conditional judgement centred on local concentration and CMA remedies.

title: Demergers
overview: A demerger is the opposite of integration: a firm splits into two or more separate businesses, usually by spinning off a division as an independent company owned by the existing shareholders. Demergers have become increasingly common among large conglomerates, from GSK's separation of its consumer health business Haleon to the break-up of General Electric. The specification asks for the reasons for demergers and their impact on businesses, workers and consumers, so exam questions usually test whether you can explain why a firm would choose to become smaller and judge who gains and who loses.
objectives: Define a demerger and distinguish it from a sale of a division (divestment)
Explain the main reasons for demergers, including diseconomies of scale, lack of synergies, the conglomerate discount, focus and regulatory pressure
Analyse the impact of demergers on businesses, workers and consumers
Evaluate whether a demerger is likely to raise efficiency, using LRAC analysis and real UK and global examples

sections.heading: What a demerger is
sections.body:
A **demerger** occurs when a single business splits into two or more separate firms. The most common method in practice is a **spin-off**: the parent company transfers a division into a new company and gives shares in it to its existing shareholders, so the same people now own two separately listed firms. Each firm then has its own board, managers, strategy, accounts and access to finance.

A related but different idea is a **divestment** (or disposal), where a firm sells a division to another company or to private equity buyers. Both make the original firm smaller and more focused, and the economic analysis of reasons and effects is similar, but in a divestment the division gains a new owner rather than becoming independent.

Demergers often reverse earlier conglomerate or horizontal integration. Many firms that grew by acquisition in the 1980s and 1990s discovered that the expected synergies did not appear, or that the combined business had become too complex to manage. Recent examples include:

- **GSK** demerged its consumer healthcare business as **Haleon** (brands such as Sensodyne and Panadol) in 2022, leaving GSK to focus on prescription medicines and vaccines.
- **Unilever** separated its ice cream business as The Magnum Ice Cream Company in 2025.
- **Kellogg** split into Kellanova (snacks) and WK Kellogg Co (North American cereals) in 2023.
- **General Electric** split into three companies focused on healthcare, energy and aviation between 2023 and 2024.
- **Prudential** demerged its UK and European arm, M&G, in 2019.

Notice that these are mainly large, diversified firms. Demergers are a response to problems that arise from size and diversity.

sections.heading: Reasons for demergers
sections.body:
Firms demerge because they believe the separate parts will be worth more, or perform better, than the whole.

- **Lack of synergies**: if two divisions share few customers, suppliers or technologies, there are no technical or purchasing economies from keeping them together. Prescription drugs and toothpaste, for example, need very different research, marketing and distribution.
- **Diseconomies of scale**: a very large, diverse organisation can suffer from coordination, communication and control problems. Decisions are slow, head office is remote from the market, and workers feel less motivated. Splitting the firm can move each part back towards its minimum efficient scale.
- **The conglomerate discount**: stock markets often value diversified groups at less than the sum of their parts, partly because investors can diversify for themselves and partly because conglomerates are hard to analyse. Separating the businesses can raise the total market value, benefiting shareholders.
- **Focus and clearer objectives**: separate management teams can concentrate on one market, set strategies suited to it and be held to account more easily, reducing the principal-agent problem.
- **Different investment and risk profiles**: a fast-growing division may want to reinvest all its profits, while a mature division generates steady cash suitable for dividends. Separate firms can attract the investors who prefer each profile and raise finance on appropriate terms.
- **Cross-subsidisation ends**: in a conglomerate, profitable divisions may fund weak ones; separation exposes poor performance and forces improvement or exit.
- **Regulation and competition policy**: competition authorities may require a firm to split or sell assets to restore competition. The Competition Commission required BAA to sell Gatwick, Stansted and Edinburgh airports between 2009 and 2013. Lloyds Banking Group had to separate TSB as a condition of state aid after the financial crisis.
- **Raising funds or deterring a takeover**: demerging a division can unlock value that might otherwise attract a predator seeking to buy and break up the firm.

sections.heading: Impact on businesses
sections.body:
**Possible benefits**

- **Lower average costs where diseconomies are removed**: simpler organisations make faster decisions and suffer fewer communication problems, reducing X-inefficiency.
- **Greater focus and dynamic efficiency**: each firm can invest in its own priorities. GSK argued that separating Haleon would allow it to devote more resources to research into new medicines.
- **Higher combined valuation**: if the conglomerate discount disappears, shareholders gain and each firm can raise capital more cheaply through its own shares.
- **Clearer accountability**: managers' performance is easier to measure, and pay can be linked to the results of a single business.

**Possible costs**

- **Loss of economies of scale**: shared services such as IT, purchasing, finance and marketing must now be duplicated, so average costs may rise. Smaller firms lose some financial and risk-bearing economies too, possibly facing higher borrowing costs.
- **One-off costs**: legal, advisory, rebranding and IT separation costs can be substantial.
- **Greater exposure to risk**: the demerged firms are less diversified, so a downturn in one market hits profits harder.
- **Vulnerability to takeover**: smaller, focused firms are easier to buy. Both parts of Kellogg were later the subject of agreed takeovers (Kellanova by Mars and WK Kellogg Co by Ferrero), showing that a demerger can be a step towards new ownership rather than lasting independence.

Whether the business gains therefore depends on the balance between removing diseconomies and losing economies of scale, which in turn depends on how much the divisions really shared.

sections.heading: Impact on workers
sections.body:
Workers can gain or lose, and the effects often differ between the two new firms.

- **Job losses**: duplicated roles may be cut, or shared functions may be restructured. If the demerged firm loses economies of scale it may seek savings through redundancies.
- **New jobs and promotion**: each new firm needs its own board, finance, HR and IT functions, creating senior and specialist roles.
- **Motivation**: workers in a smaller, focused firm may feel closer to decision-making and more valued, reducing motivational diseconomies of scale. Share schemes linked to a single business also give a clearer link between effort and reward.
- **Job security**: a less diversified firm is more exposed to shocks in its market, and a demerged firm that is later taken over may face restructuring. Conversely, a strong demerged firm that can invest in growth may offer more secure long-term employment.
- **Pay and conditions**: terms are usually protected on transfer, but the new firm may change pension arrangements or pay structures over time.

In labour market terms (3.5), demergers can also affect bargaining power: a smaller employer may have less monopsony power in a local labour market, which could support wages, while trade unions may need to negotiate with separate employers.

sections.heading: Impact on consumers
sections.body:
For consumers, the key questions are what happens to prices, quality, choice and innovation.

- **Lower prices or better quality** if the demerged firms become more efficient and focused, especially where they face competition and must pass on cost savings.
- **More innovation**: a focused firm investing in its core market may develop new products faster (dynamic efficiency). A drug company free of consumer brands may concentrate on research; a consumer goods firm may respond faster to changing tastes.
- **More competition** where a demerger is forced by regulators to break up market power. After BAA sold Gatwick and Stansted, the London airports had separate owners with an incentive to compete for airlines, and Gatwick's new owners invested heavily in terminals and services to win traffic.
- **Higher prices** if the demerged firms lose economies of scale and pass higher average costs on to consumers, or if the demerged firm is later taken over by a rival, increasing concentration.
- **Little change** in many cases: consumers buying Sensodyne toothpaste or Magnum ice creams may notice no difference at all, because brands, products and supply chains continue as before.

A strong answer recognises that the impact on consumers is often small and indirect in voluntary demergers, which are mainly driven by shareholder value, but can be large in regulator-imposed break-ups whose purpose is to increase competition.

key_terms.definition: The splitting of a single firm into two or more separate businesses, usually by spinning off a division as an independent company owned by the existing shareholders.
A form of demerger in which a parent company creates a new independent company from a division and distributes its shares to the parent's shareholders.
The sale of a division or subsidiary of a firm to another owner.
The tendency for a diversified group to be valued by investors at less than the combined value its separate businesses would have as independent firms.
The additional value created when businesses operate together rather than separately, for example through shared costs or cross-selling.
Increases in long-run average cost as a firm's scale of output rises beyond minimum efficient scale, caused by problems of coordination, communication, control and motivation.
Using profits from one part of a business to finance losses or low returns in another part.

diagrams.title: Demerger to escape diseconomies of scale
diagrams.caption: A firm producing Q1 suffers diseconomies of scale. Splitting it so that each business operates at Q2 lowers average cost to AC2 at minimum efficient scale. If the split leaves a business too small (Q3), it loses economies of scale and average cost rises.

applications: GSK and Haleon (2022): GSK separated its consumer healthcare division, which sells products such as Sensodyne and Panadol, into the independently listed Haleon. The logic was a lack of synergies: prescription medicines depend on long, risky research programmes, while consumer health depends on brands and retail distribution. Separation allowed GSK to focus spending on vaccines and specialty medicines and allowed investors to choose the risk profile they preferred.

Unilever's ice cream demerger (2025): Unilever separated its ice cream brands into The Magnum Ice Cream Company, arguing that ice cream had different characteristics from its other businesses, including a frozen supply chain, high seasonality and different capital needs. The case illustrates the lack-of-synergy and focus arguments, and the potential cost of losing shared purchasing and distribution economies.

Regulator-imposed break-up of BAA: after a Competition Commission investigation found that common ownership of the main London and Scottish airports restricted competition, BAA was required to sell Gatwick, Stansted and Edinburgh between 2009 and 2013. The separate owners invested in competing for airlines, illustrating how demergers can benefit consumers when they reduce market power.

Kellogg (2023): the split into Kellanova and WK Kellogg Co separated faster-growing snack brands from a slower-growing cereals business. Both firms were subsequently the subject of agreed takeovers by larger rivals (Mars and Ferrero), showing that demergers can make businesses easier to acquire, which may eventually increase concentration in some markets.

General Electric: once the archetypal conglomerate, GE split into GE HealthCare, GE Vernova (energy) and GE Aerospace between 2023 and 2024, after years in which the complexity of the group was widely blamed for poor decisions and weak returns. It is a strong example of diseconomies of scale and the conglomerate discount.
evaluation: The net effect on costs depends on how much the divisions genuinely shared. Where shared purchasing, logistics or technology were important, a demerger may raise costs; where the divisions were unrelated, the loss of economies of scale is small and the gains from focus dominate.

Voluntary demergers are mainly designed to raise shareholder value, so the main beneficiaries are often shareholders; effects on consumers may be negligible. Regulator-imposed demergers are designed to increase competition, so consumer gains are more likely.
Time period: one-off separation costs and possible redundancies fall in the short run, while gains from focus and innovation may take years to materialise, and some never do.
The demerged businesses may not remain independent. If they are taken over by rivals, market concentration may rise, which could harm consumers and offset the original competitive benefits.

Evidence on the conglomerate discount is mixed: some diversified groups (for example Berkshire Hathaway) have long performed strongly, suggesting that good management and efficient internal capital allocation can outweigh the costs of size and complexity.
misconceptions: Thinking a demerger means the business closes or shrinks its total output. Usually the same activities continue, but under separate ownership and management.

Assuming demergers always reduce costs. They remove diseconomies of scale only if the firm was beyond minimum efficient scale; they can also cause loss of economies of scale and duplication of overheads.
Confusing a demerger with a divestment. In a demerger (spin-off) the existing shareholders own the new firm; in a divestment the division is sold to a new owner.
Ignoring the role of regulators. Some break-ups are required by competition authorities to reduce market power, which changes the analysis of the impact on consumers.
exam_tips: Section A short questions may ask for one reason for a demerger: state the reason, link it to a concept (diseconomies of scale, lack of synergies, conglomerate discount) and apply it to the firm in the stimulus.
The specification names three stakeholder groups for impact: businesses, workers and consumers. Structure answers around them and make sure you consider both positive and negative effects for each.
Use an LRAC diagram to show a demerger moving a firm from a point of diseconomies of scale back towards MES, but evaluate by noting that a firm could overshoot and lose economies of scale.
Link demergers to earlier topics: they often reverse conglomerate integration (3.1.2), address the principal-agent problem (3.1.1) and can raise efficiency (3.4.1) or contestability (3.4.7).

model_answer.question: A large food and household goods conglomerate plans to demerge its food division into a separate company. Assess the likely impact of the demerger on workers and consumers. (12 marks)
model_answer.answer:
A demerger is when a single firm splits into two or more independent businesses, typically by spinning off a division whose shares are given to existing shareholders. Here the food division would become a separate company from the household goods business.

For workers, one likely effect is a change in job security. Shared functions such as purchasing, IT, finance and logistics previously served both divisions. After the demerger each firm must either duplicate these functions or buy them in, which raises costs. To restore profit margins, the new firms may restructure and cut jobs, especially in head office. On the other hand, the new food company needs its own board and specialist departments, which creates new senior roles. Workers may also become more motivated: in a smaller, focused firm, communication is better and staff can see how their work affects results, reducing motivational diseconomies of scale. If the firm uses share schemes, rewards are now linked to the performance of the business workers actually contribute to.

For consumers, the main channel is efficiency. If the conglomerate suffered diseconomies of scale, such as slow decision-making because food managers had to compete for attention and investment with household goods, then the demerger allows the food firm to respond more quickly to changing tastes, for example by developing healthier products in response to rules on high fat, salt and sugar foods. This increases dynamic efficiency and could mean better products and more choice. If the new firm moves closer to minimum efficient scale, average costs fall and, in a competitive grocery supply market where supermarkets have strong buying power, some of these savings are likely to be passed on in prices. However, if the divisions shared distribution networks and bulk purchasing of packaging and advertising, the demerged firms lose purchasing and marketing economies of scale. Average costs rise, and with branded products facing relatively price-inelastic demand, part of the cost increase could be passed on to consumers as higher prices.

The overall impact depends on several factors. First, how much the two divisions really shared: food and household cleaning products use different factories and ingredients, so technical synergies are probably small, but they do share retail customers and distribution, so some economies of scale will be lost. Second, the motive: this is a voluntary demerger likely to be driven by the conglomerate discount and shareholder value, so the effects on consumers may be modest, and many consumers will notice no change because the brands continue as before. Third, the time period: in the short run separation costs and restructuring may cause job losses, while gains from focus and innovation take longer. Finally, the demerged food firm may become a takeover target for a larger rival, which could increase concentration and reduce competition, harming consumers in the long run.

On balance, the demerger is likely to have mixed but modest effects. Workers in duplicated head-office roles are most at risk in the short term, while workers in the operating businesses may benefit from investment and clearer focus. Consumers are likely to see little direct change in the short run, with potential long-run gains from innovation if the new food firm is well managed, but these depend on it remaining independent and on competition from rivals and supermarket own brands forcing it to pass on any efficiency gains.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: accurate definition of a demerger and correct use of economies/diseconomies of scale, MES and dynamic efficiency. Application: tailored to a food and household goods conglomerate, with reference to supermarket buying power, HFSS rules and shared distribution. Analysis: clear chains for both stakeholder groups, including the link from costs and PED to prices. Evaluation: weighs economies lost against diseconomies removed, considers motive, time period and takeover risk, and gives a conditional judgement. This reaches the top level for a 12-mark question.
